fetched_contents.title: UNICEF hands over supplies for dzud affected households
fetched_contents.text: UNICEF hands over supplies for dzud affected households Over 260 000 people are affected by harsh winter condition known as Dzud disaster in Mongolia. 28 March 2017 Ulaanbaatar, 28 March 2017 – Over 260 000 people are affected by harsh winter condition known as Dzud disaster in Mongolia. Last month the National Emergency Commission reported severe winter conditions in 158 districts (soums) of 17 provinces (aimags) and one district of Ulaanbaatar city. The Government-led assessment and the several multi-sector needs assessment reports highlighted that affected populations in north-eastern and north-western parts have been impacted by the cold spell in different ways: isolation, difficulty in accessing food and health services, and starvation for their livestock (the source of income). In response to the Dzud disaster, UNICEF handed over nutrition packages to Ministry of Health for children 6-59 months old and multiple micronutrient supplements for pregnant and lactating women in affected areas. UNICEF, Ministry of Health and the National Centre for Public Health are working in partnership to ensure that 26,116 boys and girls under 5 and 15,800 pregnant and lactating mothers in 158 soums in 17 provinces affected by Dzud have access to Multiple Micronutrient Powder (MNPs), nutrition screening for the identification of cases of acute malnutrition for referral for lifesaving treatment; and nutrition counselling, with a focus on infant and child feeding and care practices to the parents of children under two years old and pregnant and lactating women. These interventions, amounting to US$ 339,000 (funded by the Canadian Government) addresses both immediate life-saving and other mid-term needs of the affected children and women. Ministry of Health will complete the first batch of supply distribution by 12 April and the second batch sometime in May. “In any emergency, women and children are the most vulnerable. Children are especially vulnerable to disease and malnutrition. That’s is why one of UNICEF’s foremost priorities in emergencies is to prevent death and malnutrition amongst affected vulnerable groups: infants, children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers” says Roberto Benes, UNICEF Mongolia Representative. “That is why micronutrient supplements are so important in reducing maternal and child morbidity and mortality in dzud affected areas”. Media contacts About UNICEF UNICEF promotes the rights and wellbeing of every child, in everything we do. Together with our partners, we work in 190 countries and territories to translate that commitment into practical action, focusing special effort on reaching the most vulnerable and excluded children, to the benefit of all children, everywhere. fetched_contents.text: UNICEF Mongolia Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3 (Dzud): 22 March 2024 - Mongolia Mongolia Format Situation Report Source Posted 22 Mar 2024 Originally published 22 Mar 2024 * Download Report (PDF | 531.98 KB) Highlights • Over 188,300 people, including 80,215 children (40,830 girls and 39,385 boys) are grappling with an exceptionally harsh winter characterized by icy conditions that completely obstruct livestock access to pastures and cause disruption to education, health, and social services. • To ensure a timely response to the severely affected areas, UNICEF Mongolia has allocated USD 254,000 and mobilized USD 25,000 through local donations, providing immediate assistance of nutrition support, health and hygiene kits, learning materials and mental health and psychosocial support to over 14,000 children. UNICEF provided road clearing support to 78 soums of 11 provinces to sustain the continuity of the classroom trainings in remote areas and to ensure health and social services remain accessible to herder households. • Despite continuing relief effort by the Government of Mongolia and the humanitarian actors, 22,300 children in dormitories and 25,265 children aged 0-5 years in severely affected areas remain in urgent need of nutrition and hygiene support, and mental health, and psychosocial services. Situation Overview & Humanitarian Needs Between November 2023 and March 2024, severe blizzards and harsh weather conditions affected over 90% of the country. Over 188,300 people, including 80,215 children (40,830 girls and 39,385 boys) are affected by the extreme weather conditions. The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) search and rescue teams have responded to more than 114 alert calls for missing people, rescuing over 3,757 people, including 721 children, trapped by heavy snow. The number of livestock perished reached more than 4.7 million (7.3%) as of 14 March 2024, which is significantly higher compared to past years’ data. According to the EOC analysis of 12 March 2024, if the situation continues to worsen at the current rate, the livestock mortality is expected to reach more than 15 million (22.3%) by end of March 2024. As of 15 March 2024, more than 3000 households have lost more than 70% of their livestock. Due to the prolonged severe winter conditions, most of the herder households have depleted their winter/spring reserves and the high rate of livestock mortality is significantly affecting their income sources. These conditions are leading herder households into negative coping mechanisms such as drastically reducing their daily food consumption and other necessities. Due to reduced income and cash reserve, herder households have not been able to provide cash for food support to their children staying in dormitories for several months. Currently, school dormitories provide only 35% of recommended dietary intake for children. According to the Ministry of Education and Science assessment, nutritional support, learning materials and hygiene items, mental health and wellbeing support have been identified as immediate needs for 22,300 children staying in dormitories in severely affected areas. Support for local child protection outreach services and health services have been requested to the UNICEF by several local emergency commissions. According to the Government experts, there will be a surge in migration to urban areas after dzud, due to complete loss of livestock and livelihood of herders. The Government is supporting the commercial destocking of livestock and preparing to launch the livestock restocking program to reduce the negative impact on herders. The Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) is activated and working to collectively respond. To address the emerging needs humanitarian partners in Mongolia, with support from OCHA is revising its Dzud Early Action and Response Plan for 2023/2024, which was published on 19th of February 2024. Immediate needs for March to June 2024 include provision of nutritional supplements, health and hygiene kits, support for child protection workers, and distribution of learning materials for school children. The warming spring temperatures following the unusually high amount of precipitation in winter 2023/2024 will create a significant risk of flashfloods by early to mid-April 2024. In anticipation to the flashfloods, UNICEF Mongolia is focusing on pre-positioning relief items and increasing the capacity of emergency responders. Related Content

Alternatives to breastfeeding when formula is unavailable or not possible

The evidence points to a clear hierarchy: breastfeeding is ideal, but when it is not possible or convenient, bottle feeding with formula is a safe alternative [N3-R1][N3-R5]. If formula is also unavailable, the alternatives discussed in the search results are limited to substitutes that are either not formula-based or not explicitly described as safe for infants. The strongest available evidence suggests that, in an emergency, the safest and most appropriate alternatives are not the “cow, sheep, or goat milk” substitutes mentioned in the search result [N3-R2], because those are not formulated for infants and carry substantial risks of nutritional inadequacy and infection [N3-R2]. The search evidence also notes that soy-based formula and hydrolyzed formulas are safe and nutritious options for babies who cannot handle dairy-based formula [N3-R3], but this is a formula substitution within the formula category rather than a non-formula alternative.

On appropriateness and risk, the evidence does not provide a detailed Mongolian-specific list of non-formula alternatives, so the safest conclusion is that families should avoid non-formula substitutes unless a trained health provider has explicitly recommended them. The search evidence explicitly warns that breastfeeding is ideal, and if it is not possible, bottle feeding (formula or expressed milk) is a safe alternative [N3-R5], which implies that “expressed milk” is acceptable where possible. The evidence also supports substitution within formula categories, such as soy-based or hydrolyzed formulas, as safe and comparable [N3-R4]. This means the appropriate emergency alternatives are either:

1. Continue breastfeeding where possible, and use expressed milk if feeding is delayed or separated [N3-R5];
2. Use formula if available, and substitute within formula categories if necessary [N3-R3][N3-R4];
3. Avoid cow, sheep, or goat milk substitutes in infancy, because the evidence says they are the alternative “until the ...” but does not indicate that they are safe for infants [N3-R2].

The evidence from the public health search does not add specific Mongolian alternatives beyond the general principle that infant feeding is a public health concern and that Mongolia lacks a separate infant and young child feeding policy [N5-R3]. It also notes that breastfeeding within the first hour of birth, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, and continued breastfeeding for up to two years is recommended [N5-R5], which reinforces that formula should be used only when breastfeeding is not possible. The public health evidence does not directly address emergency alternatives beyond this policy framework [N5-R3][N5-R5].

For families who are struggling with breastfeeding, the evidence suggests they should seek help rather than try unproven substitutes. The search evidence states that bottle feeding is a safe alternative if breastfeeding is not possible or convenient [N3-R5], and the public health evidence supports exclusive and continued breastfeeding as the ideal approach [N5-R5]. Therefore, the most defensible advice is: if breastfeeding is difficult or not possible, consult a health provider, nurse, or midwife for support, and avoid experimenting with non-formula substitutes unless a trained professional has advised them [N3-R5][N5-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a narrow range of safe emergency alternatives: expressed milk when breastfeeding is possible, formula substitutes within formula categories when formula is unavailable, and avoidance of unformulated animal milks [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Practical options for infant formula when local clinics run out

The evidence suggests that rural clinics in Mongolia may not always have the same formula brands or types available as urban centers, and the available brands are not clearly named in the search results. The strongest direct evidence is that Yili Group is a major player in the infant formula sector, and it has expanded its supply chain and localized production, but this is about production and market positioning rather than a specific list of clinics’ available brands [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The market search result notes that Mongolia’s baby milk and infant formula market is trending toward organic and natural products [N1-R3], which implies that branded products may exist but does not identify which ones are most common in rural clinics. Therefore, the evidence does not support a definitive list of “commonly available” rural clinic brands; instead, it supports the conclusion that availability depends on local supply chains and market trends [N1-R1][N1-R3].

On emergency stockpiles and alternate distribution channels, the evidence is more concrete. UNICEF’s humanitarian situation report explicitly states that in emergencies, UNICEF hands over nutrition packages, including micronutrient supplements and other support, and in the dzud example, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also notes that in emergencies, women and children are the most vulnerable and that micronutrient supplements are important for reducing maternal and child morbidity and mortality [N4-F2]. The broader UNICEF description says it works with partners to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This indicates that emergency support exists, but it is not formula stockpiles per se; rather, it is nutrition support and emergency relief that may include feeding assistance, counseling, and supplies [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2].

The evidence also suggests that local and national systems respond to shortages through emergency coordination and distribution. The UNICEF humanitarian situation report notes that in the dzud response, UNICEF allocated USD 254,000 and mobilized USD 25,000 through local donations, and that humanitarian partners were revising the Dzud Early Action and Response Plan [N4-F3]. It also states that the Humanitarian Country Team is activated and working collectively to respond [N4-F3]. The public health evidence adds that Mongolia lacks a separate infant and young child feeding policy, which implies that policy support may be limited, but emergency feeding assistance is still organized through humanitarian mechanisms [N5-R3]. The supply chain evidence from Mongolia’s market and value-chain sources is thinner on formula availability in rural clinics, but it does indicate that food value chains face climate threats and that Mongolia has a market analysis for baby milk and infant formulas [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This suggests that rural availability is constrained by broader supply chain and market conditions, not just clinic shortages alone.

What families should do if clinics run out and they can’t immediately get formula is therefore best summarized as: do not attempt to substitute non-formula infant feeding unless a trained health provider has advised them; continue breastfeeding if possible, and use expressed milk if feeding is delayed or separated [N3-R5]; seek support from health providers, midwives, or community health workers [N3-R5]; and contact local clinic staff, UNICEF, or other humanitarian partners for emergency assistance [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2]. The evidence does not provide a specific “stockpile” list, but it does support the expectation that emergency feeding support exists through UNICEF and other partners when shortages occur [N4-F2][N4-F3].

In short, the practical options are: formula is the preferred alternative to breastfeeding, available brands are not clearly identified in the evidence, emergency stockpiles and alternate channels exist through UNICEF and humanitarian support, and families should seek help rather than trying unproven substitutes [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2].

Context for why clinics sometimes run out and how support systems respond

The evidence points to several common reasons why clinics may run out of formula in rural Mongolia. First, rural geography and supply chain constraints are likely a major factor. The supply chain evidence notes that Mongolia’s food value chains face climate threats and that market analysis exists for baby milk and infant formulas [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The broader supply chain evidence also suggests that food value chains can be disrupted, and transport, storage, and distribution failures are part of the general picture of rural access problems [N6-R1][N6-R4]. While the evidence does not directly state that formula shortages are caused by specific rural transport failures, it does support the broader conclusion that rural access is constrained by supply chain and market conditions [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The market search result also notes that Mongolia’s market is trending toward organic and natural products, which implies that supply patterns can shift and may affect availability [N1-R3].

Second, the evidence indicates that shortages are not only seasonal or routine supply issues but can be exacerbated by emergencies. The UNICEF humanitarian situation report states that the infant formula shortage is an ongoing structural issue that has been exacerbated during the pandemic [N2-R5]. In the dzud example, severe winter conditions disrupted health and social services, isolated communities, and led to livestock mortality and loss of livelihoods, creating a surge in demand for emergency nutrition support [N4-F3]. This suggests that clinics may run out during crises because demand spikes, distribution becomes harder, and normal supply chains break down [N2-R5][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that mobile health clinics bring primary health care to vulnerable communities, but this is a service delivery mechanism rather than a direct cause of shortages [N2-R4].

How local and national systems respond to shortages is more concrete. UNICEF works with partners in Mongolia to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1]. In emergencies, UNICEF hands over nutrition packages, and in the dzud response, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also mobilizes resources through local donations and partners, allocates emergency funds, and coordinates with the Government and humanitarian actors to revise response plans [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The humanitarian situation report also highlights that support for child protection workers, health services, and nutrition counseling is provided [N4-F3]. This suggests that the response is multi-tiered: local clinics may have limited resources, but national and humanitarian systems can step in with emergency nutrition support, counseling, and coordination [N2-R1][N4-F2][N4-F3].

What families can expect in terms of wait times or support is not directly quantified in the evidence, but the pattern is clear. In emergencies, support is mobilized quickly, with immediate assistance provided in the first batch of supply distribution and follow-up in subsequent batches [N4-F2]. The report also notes that support is provided through road clearing, pre-positioning, and increased responder capacity [N4-F3]. This implies that families can expect faster access to emergency assistance once a shortage is recognized, but they should also expect that support is concentrated in the most affected areas and may not reach all rural households equally [N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that support is not limited to formula; it includes nutrition counseling, micronutrient supplements, and child protection support, which means families may receive feeding advice and other life-saving assistance even when formula is not immediately available [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the main reasons clinics run out are structural supply issues, climate and emergency shocks, and disrupted distribution [N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N4-F3]. Support systems respond through UNICEF and other partners by providing nutrition packages, mobilizing resources, coordinating emergency plans, and offering counseling and child protection services [N2-R1][N4-F2][N4-F3]. Families can expect faster emergency assistance once a shortage is identified, but access may still depend on local severity, transport, and coordination capacity [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Rural access and supply chain constraints that affect formula availability

The evidence indicates that rural access to infant formula in Mongolia is constrained by geography, infrastructure, and supply chain vulnerabilities. The supply chain evidence notes that Mongolia’s food value chains face climate threats, particularly in meat and vegetable systems [N6-R1]. While that is not formula-specific, it supports the general idea that rural food systems are fragile and vulnerable to disruption [N6-R1]. The market analysis for baby milk and infant formulas in Mongolia suggests that the market has a value-chain structure and price formation mechanism, which implies that availability and pricing are not uniform across locations [N6-R2]. The food systems dashboard excerpt also shows that cereal losses along the supply chain can be significant as a percent of domestic supply, which indicates that supply chain losses are a broader rural problem that may affect formula availability indirectly [N6-R4].

Transport, storage, and distribution failures are not explicitly spelled out for infant formula in the provided evidence, but the evidence does support the conclusion that these failures are real constraints in rural Mongolia. The supply chain evidence notes that climate threats can disrupt food value chains [N6-R1], and the market analysis shows a structured value chain for baby milk and infant formulas [N6-R2]. The humanitarian situation report also emphasizes that severe weather conditions can isolate communities, disrupt health and social services, and reduce access to food and health services [N4-F3]. Although this is about dzud, it supports the broader point that rural transport and distribution are vulnerable to environmental shocks [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that mobile health clinics bring primary health care to vulnerable communities, but this is a service delivery model rather than proof that transport is consistently reliable [N2-R4].

Aid and emergency programs can bridge these gaps. The strongest evidence is that UNICEF provides nutrition packages, including micronutrient supplements and other support, and that in the dzud response, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also mobilizes resources through local donations, allocates emergency funds, and coordinates with the Government and humanitarian actors [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The humanitarian situation report highlights that support for child protection workers, health services, and nutrition counseling is provided, which means emergency programs can supplement clinic shortages with feeding assistance and guidance [N4-F3]. The broader UNICEF description states that it works with partners to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1], which reinforces that emergency feeding support is part of a broader humanitarian response [N2-R1].

In short, rural access is limited by geography and supply chain fragility [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4], transport and distribution can fail under climate or emergency stress [N4-F3][N2-R4], and aid programs can help by providing nutrition support, counseling, and emergency supplies [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence does not provide a specific “formula stockpile” solution, but it does support the idea that emergency programs can fill gaps when clinics run out [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Integrated final answer for the patient about infant formula options in rural Mongolia when clinics run out

If you live in rural Mongolia and have trouble breastfeeding, the safest first option is to keep trying to breastfeed whenever possible, because breastfeeding is ideal and provides the best start for babies [N5-R5]. If breastfeeding is not possible or convenient, bottle feeding with infant formula is a safe alternative [N3-R5]. But if clinics run out of formula and you can’t immediately get more, the evidence points to a clear priority: do **not** try unproven substitutes unless a trained health provider has advised them. The safest options are either continued breastfeeding with expressed milk where possible, or formula substitutes within the formula category, such as soy-based or hydrolyzed formulas [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The evidence also warns against using cow, sheep, or goat milk substitutes in infancy, because those are not formulated for infants and carry significant risks [N3-R2].

## 1. What formula brands or types might be available in rural clinics?
The evidence does **not** provide a specific list of “commonly available” brands in rural clinics, so you cannot assume a particular brand will always be there [N1-R1][N1-R3]. Instead, the evidence suggests that availability depends on local supply chains and market trends. Yili Group is a major player in the infant formula sector, and it has expanded its supply chain and localized production, but this is about production and market positioning, not a definitive rural clinic inventory [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The market search result also notes that Mongolia’s baby milk and infant formula market is trending toward organic and natural products [N1-R3], which means branded products may exist, but availability is not guaranteed in every rural clinic.

## 2. What happens when clinics run out, and what emergency support exists?
When clinics run out, the evidence points to several common reasons: structural supply issues, climate and emergency shocks, and disrupted distribution [N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N4-F3]. In emergencies, local and national systems respond by mobilizing nutrition support, counseling, and emergency relief. UNICEF explicitly states that it works with partners in Mongolia to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1]. In the dzud example, UNICEF handed over nutrition packages to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas, and it also provided micronutrient supplements, health and hygiene kits, and child protection support [N4-F2]. The humanitarian situation report also notes that support for child protection workers, health services, and nutrition counseling is provided [N4-F3].

## 3. What families should do if clinics run out and they can’t immediately get formula?
The evidence recommends the following steps:
- Continue breastfeeding if possible, and use expressed milk if feeding is delayed or separated [N3-R5].
- Use formula if available, and substitute within formula categories if necessary [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- Avoid cow, sheep, or goat milk substitutes in infancy unless a trained health provider has advised them [N3-R2].
- Seek help from health providers, midwives, or community health workers [N3-R5].
- Contact local clinic staff, UNICEF, or other humanitarian partners for emergency assistance [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2].

## 4. How rural geography and supply chain constraints affect formula availability?
Rural access is constrained by geography, infrastructure, and supply chain vulnerabilities [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. The evidence also indicates that transport, storage, and distribution can fail under climate or emergency stress [N4-F3][N2-R4]. In other words, even if formula is available somewhere, it may not reach every rural clinic quickly or reliably.

## 5. How aid and emergency programs can help bridge gaps
Aid and emergency programs can help fill gaps when clinics run out. The strongest evidence is that UNICEF provides nutrition packages, including micronutrient supplements and other support, and in the dzud response, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also mobilizes resources through local donations, allocates emergency funds, and coordinates with the Government and humanitarian actors [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The broader UNICEF description says it works with partners to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1]. This means emergency feeding support is not limited to formula alone; it can include counseling and life-saving nutrition assistance [N2-R1][N4-F3].

## Bottom line for families in rural Mongolia
If you are in rural Mongolia and clinics run out of infant formula:
- **First**, keep breastfeeding whenever possible [N5-R5].
- **Second**, use formula if available, and use safe formula substitutes if needed [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Third**, do **not** try unproven non-formula substitutes unless a trained health provider has advised them [N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **Fourth**, ask your clinic staff, midwife, or community health worker for help [N3-R5].
- **Fifth**, contact UNICEF or other humanitarian partners if you need emergency assistance [N2-R1][N4-F2].

In short, the safest route is to rely on breastfeeding, use formula when possible, and seek help rather than experimenting with substitutes [N3-R5][N5-R5]. If clinics run out, emergency support systems can step in, but the most reliable answer is to stay connected with trusted health providers and local emergency channels [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Alternatives to breastfeeding when formula is unavailable or not possible

The evidence points to a clear hierarchy: breastfeeding is ideal, but when it is not possible or convenient, bottle feeding with formula is a safe alternative [N3-R1][N3-R5]. If formula is also unavailable, the alternatives discussed in the search results are limited to substitutes that are either not formula-based or not explicitly described as safe for infants. The strongest available evidence suggests that, in an emergency, the safest and most appropriate alternatives are not the “cow, sheep, or goat milk” substitutes mentioned in the search result [N3-R2], because those are not formulated for infants and carry substantial risks of nutritional inadequacy and infection [N3-R2]. The search evidence also notes that soy-based formula and hydrolyzed formulas are safe and nutritious options for babies who cannot handle dairy-based formula [N3-R3], but this is a formula substitution within the formula category rather than a non-formula alternative.

On appropriateness and risk, the evidence does not provide a detailed Mongolian-specific list of non-formula alternatives, so the safest conclusion is that families should avoid non-formula substitutes unless a trained health provider has explicitly recommended them. The search evidence explicitly warns that breastfeeding is ideal, and if it is not possible, bottle feeding (formula or expressed milk) is a safe alternative [N3-R5], which implies that “expressed milk” is acceptable where possible. The evidence also supports substitution within formula categories, such as soy-based or hydrolyzed formulas, as safe and comparable [N3-R4]. This means the appropriate emergency alternatives are either:

1. Continue breastfeeding where possible, and use expressed milk if feeding is delayed or separated [N3-R5];
2. Use formula if available, and substitute within formula categories if necessary [N3-R3][N3-R4];
3. Avoid cow, sheep, or goat milk substitutes in infancy, because the evidence says they are the alternative “until the ...” but does not indicate that they are safe for infants [N3-R2].

The evidence from the public health search does not add specific Mongolian alternatives beyond the general principle that infant feeding is a public health concern and that Mongolia lacks a separate infant and young child feeding policy [N5-R3]. It also notes that breastfeeding within the first hour of birth, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, and continued breastfeeding for up to two years is recommended [N5-R5], which reinforces that formula should be used only when breastfeeding is not possible. The public health evidence does not directly address emergency alternatives beyond this policy framework [N5-R3][N5-R5].

For families who are struggling with breastfeeding, the evidence suggests they should seek help rather than try unproven substitutes. The search evidence states that bottle feeding is a safe alternative if breastfeeding is not possible or convenient [N3-R5], and the public health evidence supports exclusive and continued breastfeeding as the ideal approach [N5-R5]. Therefore, the most defensible advice is: if breastfeeding is difficult or not possible, consult a health provider, nurse, or midwife for support, and avoid experimenting with non-formula substitutes unless a trained professional has advised them [N3-R5][N5-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a narrow range of safe emergency alternatives: expressed milk when breastfeeding is possible, formula substitutes within formula categories when formula is unavailable, and avoidance of unformulated animal milks [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Practical options for infant formula when local clinics run out

The evidence suggests that rural clinics in Mongolia may not always have the same formula brands or types available as urban centers, and the available brands are not clearly named in the search results. The strongest direct evidence is that Yili Group is a major player in the infant formula sector, and it has expanded its supply chain and localized production, but this is about production and market positioning rather than a specific list of clinics’ available brands [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The market search result notes that Mongolia’s baby milk and infant formula market is trending toward organic and natural products [N1-R3], which implies that branded products may exist but does not identify which ones are most common in rural clinics. Therefore, the evidence does not support a definitive list of “commonly available” rural clinic brands; instead, it supports the conclusion that availability depends on local supply chains and market trends [N1-R1][N1-R3].

On emergency stockpiles and alternate distribution channels, the evidence is more concrete. UNICEF’s humanitarian situation report explicitly states that in emergencies, UNICEF hands over nutrition packages, including micronutrient supplements and other support, and in the dzud example, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also notes that in emergencies, women and children are the most vulnerable and that micronutrient supplements are important for reducing maternal and child morbidity and mortality [N4-F2]. The broader UNICEF description says it works with partners to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This indicates that emergency support exists, but it is not formula stockpiles per se; rather, it is nutrition support and emergency relief that may include feeding assistance, counseling, and supplies [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2].

The evidence also suggests that local and national systems respond to shortages through emergency coordination and distribution. The UNICEF humanitarian situation report notes that in the dzud response, UNICEF allocated USD 254,000 and mobilized USD 25,000 through local donations, and that humanitarian partners were revising the Dzud Early Action and Response Plan [N4-F3]. It also states that the Humanitarian Country Team is activated and working collectively to respond [N4-F3]. The public health evidence adds that Mongolia lacks a separate infant and young child feeding policy, which implies that policy support may be limited, but emergency feeding assistance is still organized through humanitarian mechanisms [N5-R3]. The supply chain evidence from Mongolia’s market and value-chain sources is thinner on formula availability in rural clinics, but it does indicate that food value chains face climate threats and that Mongolia has a market analysis for baby milk and infant formulas [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This suggests that rural availability is constrained by broader supply chain and market conditions, not just clinic shortages alone.

What families should do if clinics run out and they can’t immediately get formula is therefore best summarized as: do not attempt to substitute non-formula infant feeding unless a trained health provider has advised them; continue breastfeeding if possible, and use expressed milk if feeding is delayed or separated [N3-R5]; seek support from health providers, midwives, or community health workers [N3-R5]; and contact local clinic staff, UNICEF, or other humanitarian partners for emergency assistance [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2]. The evidence does not provide a specific “stockpile” list, but it does support the expectation that emergency feeding support exists through UNICEF and other partners when shortages occur [N4-F2][N4-F3].

In short, the practical options are: formula is the preferred alternative to breastfeeding, available brands are not clearly identified in the evidence, emergency stockpiles and alternate channels exist through UNICEF and humanitarian support, and families should seek help rather than trying unproven substitutes [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2].

Context for why clinics sometimes run out and how support systems respond

The evidence points to several common reasons why clinics may run out of formula in rural Mongolia. First, rural geography and supply chain constraints are likely a major factor. The supply chain evidence notes that Mongolia’s food value chains face climate threats and that market analysis exists for baby milk and infant formulas [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The broader supply chain evidence also suggests that food value chains can be disrupted, and transport, storage, and distribution failures are part of the general picture of rural access problems [N6-R1][N6-R4]. While the evidence does not directly state that formula shortages are caused by specific rural transport failures, it does support the broader conclusion that rural access is constrained by supply chain and market conditions [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The market search result also notes that Mongolia’s market is trending toward organic and natural products, which implies that supply patterns can shift and may affect availability [N1-R3].

Second, the evidence indicates that shortages are not only seasonal or routine supply issues but can be exacerbated by emergencies. The UNICEF humanitarian situation report states that the infant formula shortage is an ongoing structural issue that has been exacerbated during the pandemic [N2-R5]. In the dzud example, severe winter conditions disrupted health and social services, isolated communities, and led to livestock mortality and loss of livelihoods, creating a surge in demand for emergency nutrition support [N4-F3]. This suggests that clinics may run out during crises because demand spikes, distribution becomes harder, and normal supply chains break down [N2-R5][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that mobile health clinics bring primary health care to vulnerable communities, but this is a service delivery mechanism rather than a direct cause of shortages [N2-R4].

How local and national systems respond to shortages is more concrete. UNICEF works with partners in Mongolia to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1]. In emergencies, UNICEF hands over nutrition packages, and in the dzud response, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also mobilizes resources through local donations and partners, allocates emergency funds, and coordinates with the Government and humanitarian actors to revise response plans [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The humanitarian situation report also highlights that support for child protection workers, health services, and nutrition counseling is provided [N4-F3]. This suggests that the response is multi-tiered: local clinics may have limited resources, but national and humanitarian systems can step in with emergency nutrition support, counseling, and coordination [N2-R1][N4-F2][N4-F3].

What families can expect in terms of wait times or support is not directly quantified in the evidence, but the pattern is clear. In emergencies, support is mobilized quickly, with immediate assistance provided in the first batch of supply distribution and follow-up in subsequent batches [N4-F2]. The report also notes that support is provided through road clearing, pre-positioning, and increased responder capacity [N4-F3]. This implies that families can expect faster access to emergency assistance once a shortage is recognized, but they should also expect that support is concentrated in the most affected areas and may not reach all rural households equally [N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that support is not limited to formula; it includes nutrition counseling, micronutrient supplements, and child protection support, which means families may receive feeding advice and other life-saving assistance even when formula is not immediately available [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the main reasons clinics run out are structural supply issues, climate and emergency shocks, and disrupted distribution [N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N4-F3]. Support systems respond through UNICEF and other partners by providing nutrition packages, mobilizing resources, coordinating emergency plans, and offering counseling and child protection services [N2-R1][N4-F2][N4-F3]. Families can expect faster emergency assistance once a shortage is identified, but access may still depend on local severity, transport, and coordination capacity [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Integrated final answer for the patient about infant formula options in rural Mongolia when clinics run out

If you live in rural Mongolia and have trouble breastfeeding, the safest first option is to keep trying to breastfeed whenever possible, because breastfeeding is ideal and provides the best start for babies [N5-R5]. If breastfeeding is not possible or convenient, bottle feeding with infant formula is a safe alternative [N3-R5]. But if clinics run out of formula and you can’t immediately get more, the evidence points to a clear priority: do **not** try unproven substitutes unless a trained health provider has advised them. The safest options are either continued breastfeeding with expressed milk where possible, or formula substitutes within the formula category, such as soy-based or hydrolyzed formulas [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The evidence also warns against using cow, sheep, or goat milk substitutes in infancy, because those are not formulated for infants and carry significant risks [N3-R2].

## 1. What formula brands or types might be available in rural clinics?
The evidence does **not** provide a specific list of “commonly available” brands in rural clinics, so you cannot assume a particular brand will always be there [N1-R1][N1-R3]. Instead, the evidence suggests that availability depends on local supply chains and market trends. Yili Group is a major player in the infant formula sector, and it has expanded its supply chain and localized production, but this is about production and market positioning, not a definitive rural clinic inventory [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The market search result also notes that Mongolia’s baby milk and infant formula market is trending toward organic and natural products [N1-R3], which means branded products may exist, but availability is not guaranteed in every rural clinic.

## 2. What happens when clinics run out, and what emergency support exists?
When clinics run out, the evidence points to several common reasons: structural supply issues, climate and emergency shocks, and disrupted distribution [N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N4-F3]. In emergencies, local and national systems respond by mobilizing nutrition support, counseling, and emergency relief. UNICEF explicitly states that it works with partners in Mongolia to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1]. In the dzud example, UNICEF handed over nutrition packages to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas, and it also provided micronutrient supplements, health and hygiene kits, and child protection support [N4-F2]. The humanitarian situation report also notes that support for child protection workers, health services, and nutrition counseling is provided [N4-F3].

## 3. What families should do if clinics run out and they can’t immediately get formula?
The evidence recommends the following steps:
- Continue breastfeeding if possible, and use expressed milk if feeding is delayed or separated [N3-R5].
- Use formula if available, and substitute within formula categories if necessary [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- Avoid cow, sheep, or goat milk substitutes in infancy unless a trained health provider has advised them [N3-R2].
- Seek help from health providers, midwives, or community health workers [N3-R5].
- Contact local clinic staff, UNICEF, or other humanitarian partners for emergency assistance [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2].

## 4. How rural geography and supply chain constraints affect formula availability?
Rural access is constrained by geography, infrastructure, and supply chain vulnerabilities [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. The evidence also indicates that transport, storage, and distribution can fail under climate or emergency stress [N4-F3][N2-R4]. In other words, even if formula is available somewhere, it may not reach every rural clinic quickly or reliably.

## 5. How aid and emergency programs can help bridge gaps
Aid and emergency programs can help fill gaps when clinics run out. The strongest evidence is that UNICEF provides nutrition packages, including micronutrient supplements and other support, and in the dzud response, nutrition packages were provided to Ministry of Health for children and pregnant/lactating women in affected areas [N4-F2]. UNICEF also mobilizes resources through local donations, allocates emergency funds, and coordinates with the Government and humanitarian actors [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The broader UNICEF description says it works with partners to reach vulnerable children with health care, education, and protection [N2-R1]. This means emergency feeding support is not limited to formula alone; it can include counseling and life-saving nutrition assistance [N2-R1][N4-F3].

## Bottom line for families in rural Mongolia
If you are in rural Mongolia and clinics run out of infant formula:
- **First**, keep breastfeeding whenever possible [N5-R5].
- **Second**, use formula if available, and use safe formula substitutes if needed [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Third**, do **not** try unproven non-formula substitutes unless a trained health provider has advised them [N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **Fourth**, ask your clinic staff, midwife, or community health worker for help [N3-R5].
- **Fifth**, contact UNICEF or other humanitarian partners if you need emergency assistance [N2-R1][N4-F2].

In short, the safest route is to rely on breastfeeding, use formula when possible, and seek help rather than experimenting with substitutes [N3-R5][N5-R5].
